cues.text: A Faith the State Had Outlawed
Christianity had arrived in Korea in the late eighteenth century through an extraordinary and genuinely unique path.
Korean scholars visiting China encountered Catholic texts translated into Chinese, and brought the faith home themselves.

They established a Christian community that grew for years under entirely lay leadership, without a single ordained priest present anywhere in the kingdom, before any missionary ever set foot in Korea.

Andrew Kim Taegon was born into this young, embattled Church in 1821 to a noble family that had converted to the outlawed faith, a decision that would eventually cost his own father, Ignatius Kim , his life in the 1839 persecution .
A Thousand Miles to Become a Priest
Baptized at fourteen or fifteen, Andrew resolved to pursue the priesthood despite the complete absence of any seminary or ordained clergy within Korea itself.
He undertook an arduous overland journey of some thirteen hundred miles to reach the Portuguese colony of Macau.
There, he began his theological studies, later completing his formation in the Philippines before returning to the region for ordination.
The First Native Korean Priest
Andrew was ordained a priest at Shanghai on August 17, 1845, by the French bishop Jean-Joseph Ferréol.
He thereby became the very first Korean ever raised to the Catholic priesthood, marking a milestone of real significance for a Church.
Until that moment, it had depended entirely on lay catechists and occasional foreign missionaries smuggled across a heavily guarded border.
Smuggling Missionaries Into a Closed Kingdom
Rather than settle into quiet parish ministry, Andrew undertook the dangerous work of arranging safe passage for additional foreign missionaries into Korea.
Korea was a kingdom that regarded Christianity as both a religious and a political threat and enforced its prohibition with real, repeated bloodshed.
In June 1846, while organizing a sea route for further missionaries along the southeast coast, Andrew was captured by a border patrol.
A Martyr's Final Letter
While awaiting trial and execution, Andrew wrote a final letter to his scattered parish community.
He framed his own coming death as a continuation of a suffering that had marked the Korean Church from its earliest days.
That letter has since become one of the most cherished testimonies of the entire Korean Catholic martyr tradition.
Legacy
Andrew was beheaded at Saenamteo, near modern Seoul, on September 16, 1846, at only twenty-five years old, after barely a year of active priestly ministry.
Andrew Kim Taegon was canonized in 1984, together with 102 other Korean martyrs, by Pope John Paul II .
It was the first canonization ceremony the pope ever held outside the Vatican.
Andrew remains patron of the Korean clergy, honored alongside a Church that would ultimately produce some ten thousand martyrs across the nineteenth century.
